## Data prepared; model fitting has not started

This page was prepared without examining results from the rebuilt H01 models.
It records what the manuscript reported, states the approved parts of the main
method, and defines a sensitivity that applies the same new method to the
dataset prepared for the manuscript. The H01 input data now pass their checks.
The author approved the complete 17-metric response-family package and the
formal fourth 17-test site-versus-latitude family before fitting. No rebuilt
H01 exposure model has yet been fitted.

:::

## Question and comparison being estimated

The recognizable H01 question remains whether personal light-exposure metrics
differ across the observed sites and whether the between-site pattern can be
adequately summarized by observed photoperiod---the time from civil dawn to
civil dusk, used here as day length---and a linear latitude gradient.

The approved primary analysis estimates differences among the observed sites
in the near-eye sample after accounting for day length. It gives each site
equal weight and averages over the day lengths observed during data collection.
It does not estimate a residual site difference after adjustment for latitude:
each site has only one latitude, so separate effects of latitude and a fixed
effect for every site cannot be estimated in the same model.

In this page, a fixed site effect estimates a separate difference for each
observed site. A participant random effect accounts for repeated days from the
same participant. A random site effect instead estimates variation among sites
while treating the observed sites as a sample from a broader population.
Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) correction adjusts a declared set of related
\(p\)-values together to limit the expected false-discovery rate: the expected
share of false positives among results declared statistically significant.

### Results reported from that method

These are claims from the submitted manuscript that still need to be checked;
they are not verified results from the audited analysis. A common sample means
that both estimates use exactly the same participants and participant-days,
where one participant-day is one participant observed on one calendar day.
\(R^2\) summarizes how much variation is represented by a model. Marginal
\(R^2\) covers the fixed effects, whereas conditional \(R^2\) covers both fixed
and random effects; differences between these quantities are not automatically
additive or causal contributions.

| Submitted claim | Reported result | Review status |
|---|---|---|
| Site differences | Level- and timing-based metrics showed site differences after photoperiod adjustment (all p ≤ 0.04); first light timing above 250 lx melEDI did not (p = 0.40). Duration-, dynamics-, exposure-history-, and spectrum-based metrics showed no site differences; the submitted manuscript reports that all of their adjusted p-values were at least 0.062 and therefore greater than 0.05. | Exact submitted model/result extraction pending. |
| Site contrasts | Kumasi had lower daytime, nighttime, and full-day melEDI; selected sites differed in timing and nighttime levels. | Contrast estimates will be reconstructed from the submitted files, and the observations shared by the submitted and audited analyses will be identified. |
| Fixed versus random site | A random site effect was supported in 5 of 7 models with a supported fixed site effect and was preferable only for full-day and nighttime levels. | The model-comparison method and use of the same observations in each comparison require verification. |
| Latitude | A 10-degree latitude increase was associated with 1.15-fold higher full-day and 1.24-fold higher daytime melEDI; latitude models reportedly fit those outcomes better than site models. | The reported estimates will be retained for direct comparison; interpretation must reflect that separate site and latitude effects cannot be estimated in the same model. |
| Photoperiod | Reported effects included factors of 1.10--1.17 for durations above thresholds, 1.19 for melEDI dose, 1.09--1.25 for level metrics, +0.02 MDER, and later mean and last timing above 250 lx melEDI. | Exact estimates, intervals, family membership, and adjusted \(p\)-values require reconstruction. |
| Explained variation | Conditional \(R^2\) ranged from 25% to 62% (mean 40%); fixed effects reportedly explained 2%--24%, participant differences 9%--42%, and site more than photoperiod when significant. | Full-model \(R^2\) will be verified; overlapping differences will not be called additive variance contributions. |

## Manuscript-prepared-data sensitivity

The same new H01 implementation described below will also be applied to the
dataset prepared for the manuscript, with only objectively demonstrable data
errors corrected. The model definitions, multiplicity families,
confidence-interval methods, diagnostics, and reporting code remain identical
to the main analysis. Only the prepared dataset changes.

This sensitivity isolates the effect of the new data-preparation and metric
rules. It does not rerun the manuscript's modelling code. Differences between
that full manuscript-generating chain and the main analysis remain part of the
audit discussion above.

## Main analysis

A common-sample placement comparison will use exactly the same participant-days
for the near-eye and chest calculations. It therefore assesses placement
differences without allowing unequal data availability to create an apparent
difference.

### Approved model for each metric

Different metrics have different distributions. For example, exposure levels
are strongly right-skewed, several duration measures contain exact zeros, and
clock times may cross midnight. One error distribution should therefore not be
forced onto all 17 outcomes.

The recommended package below preserves the manuscript's model choices as far
as possible and fixes the model for each metric before any site, day-length or
latitude effect is examined. “Normal after log transformation” means that
`log10(value + 0.1)` is modelled with normally distributed errors; adding 0.1
retains exact zeros. A Tweedie model is a continuous model that permits exact
zeros and right-skewed positive values; its log link reports effects as ratios.
An identity model reports effects as ordinary differences.

| Metric | Recommended primary model | Why this is the starting choice | Required check or predefined alternative |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interdaily stability | Normal errors after a logit transformation | IS is bounded between 0 and 1; no value is at either boundary. | Check the transformed residuals. A beta model would be a major method change. |
| Intradaily variability | Normal errors, identity scale | The observed range is not bounded near zero and is approximately symmetric. | Check residual spread and influential participants. |
| Mean melEDI | Normal errors after `log10(value + 0.1)` | Preserves the recognizable zero-aware analysis of a strongly right-skewed exposure level. | Check the upper tail and sensitivity to the 0.1-lx offset; Tweedie is the named alternative. |
| Brightest 10-hour mean melEDI | Normal errors after `log10(value + 0.1)` | Preserves the analysis while accommodating the long upper tail. | Strong influence and upper-tail checks; Tweedie is the named alternative. |
| Darkest 10-hour mean melEDI | Normal errors after `log10(value + 0.1)` | Preserves the analysis and retains the 111 near-eye days with a value of zero. | This is a high-risk fit because 13.7% of near-eye values are zero; Tweedie is the named alternative. |
| Time above 1,000 lx melEDI | Tweedie errors with a log link | The duration is non-negative, right-skewed and sometimes exactly zero. | Check the predicted zero frequency, upper tail and impossible predictions outside 0–24 hours. |
| Time above 250 lx melEDI during wake | Tweedie errors with a log link | The duration is non-negative, right-skewed and sometimes zero. | Check predictions against each day's waking duration. Modelling a proportion would change the question and requires approval. |
| Time below 10 lx melEDI before sleep | Tweedie errors with a log link | The duration is non-negative and can be zero. | Check the three-hour ceiling; a shifted-log normal model is the named alternative. |
| Time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep | Tweedie errors with a log link | Preserves the manuscript model for a non-negative duration. | This distribution is less clearly right-skewed; an identity-scale normal model is the predefined alternative. Switching the primary model requires approval. |
| Longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI | Normal errors after `log10(value + 0.1)` | Preserves the recognizable model for the observed lower bound. | An analysis restricted to exactly identified periods is mandatory; an interval-censored model would change the outcome and requires approval. |
| Midpoint of the brightest 10 hours | Normal errors, identity scale | Values remain within the daytime and behave linearly. | Check that the fitted sample remains away from the clock boundary. |
| Midpoint of the darkest 10 hours | Normal errors after moving evening values before midnight onto a negative-hour scale | The darkest period crosses midnight; subtracting 24 hours from values after noon creates one continuous nighttime scale. | Confirm that both datasets remain centred around midnight. A circular model is needed only if that check fails. |
| Mean timing above 250 lx melEDI | Normal errors, identity scale | The observed times lie on one continuous daytime-to-evening scale. | Confirm that no fitted sample crosses the chosen clock boundary. |
| First light timing above 250 lx melEDI | Normal errors, identity scale | Values are concentrated from midnight into the morning, without a second late-evening cluster. | Confirm this one-sided pattern in both datasets. |
| Last light timing above 250 lx melEDI | Normal errors, identity scale | Values are concentrated from morning to midnight, without a second early-morning cluster. | Confirm this one-sided pattern in both datasets. |
| melEDI dose | Normal errors after `log10(value + 0.1)` | Preserves the recognizable analysis while accommodating a long upper tail and exact zeros. | Strong influence and upper-tail checks; Tweedie is the named alternative. |
| MDER | Normal errors, identity scale | MDER is not restricted to 0–1; the chest data include zero and values above 1, so a beta model is invalid. | Check the lower tail and influential sites or participants; zero-capable Tweedie is the named alternative. |

The same approved primary model must be used for the main and
manuscript-prepared datasets. If it fails required checks in one dataset, that
result is reported as non-estimable until the author approves a common
replacement; the two data scenarios will not be given different models.

### Approved multiple-testing families

The correction uses one preselected test from each metric model, not every
coefficient in that model. A likelihood-ratio test compares two models fitted
to the same observations that differ only in the predictor being tested. The
approved H01 families are:

- **Site:** for each of the 17 metrics, one overall test comparing the model
  with site and day length against the model with day length alone. This asks
  whether site improves the model as a whole, rather than testing every site
  coefficient separately.
- **Day length:** for each metric, one test comparing the model with site and
  day length against the model with site alone.
- **Latitude:** for each metric, one test comparing the model with latitude
  and day length against the model with day length alone.
- **Site versus latitude:** for each metric, one formal same-frame comparison
  between the full site-factor model and the otherwise identical
  linear-latitude model. This tests whether one latitude gradient adequately
  summarizes the full site pattern.

Each comparison produces one \(p\)-value per metric. BH correction is then
applied once to each of the four separate 17-value vectors. Individual site contrasts and
other follow-up parameters are not added to these primary vectors; any formal
tests of those parameters require a separately declared secondary correction.
The descriptive random-site analysis is not part of any of these four
families.

### Approved formal test of latitude adequacy

The three approved 17-test families answer whether site, day length and
latitude improve their respective models. They do **not** directly test
whether a single linear latitude gradient is an adequate summary of the
full between-site pattern.

For each metric, the site-factor model will be compared with the otherwise
identical linear-latitude model on exactly the same observations. The 17
model-level \(p\)-values form the approved fourth BH family. This permits a
formal statement about whether latitude adequately summarizes the site
pattern. Same-sample AIC differences and leave-one-site-out latitude estimates
remain descriptive supporting analyses.

For a metric whose overall site test is supported after the 17-test
correction, the site follow-up uses the `emmeans` effect contrast: each site is
compared with the mean of all site averages, with every site weighted equally.
The nine near-eye follow-up p-values form a separate family for that metric
and are adjusted together; the complementary chest analysis has eight
site deviations and adjusts those eight values together. On a log scale the
follow-up is reported as a ratio; on a linear scale it is reported as a
difference. Both are accompanied by 95% confidence intervals. Metrics without
a supported overall site test do not receive inferential site follow-ups,
matching the hierarchy used in the submitted H1 table.

### How variation will be described

The submitted percentages remain unverified reported results. The repaired
analysis will separate overall model performance from predictor-specific
contributions:

- **Marginal \(R^2\)** describes the variation represented by site and day
  length together.
- **Conditional \(R^2\)** additionally includes persistent differences among
  participants. Their difference is reported as the participant-associated
  share for participant-day models. IS and IV have one value per participant,
  so they cannot estimate a participant random-effect share.
- **Part \(R^2\) for site** is the loss in fixed-effect prediction variance
  when the whole site term is removed from the same model.
- **Part \(R^2\) for day length** is calculated in the same way after removing
  day length.
- The latitude model receives its own part \(R^2\) for latitude; it is not
  added to the fixed-site model's quantities.
- One minus conditional \(R^2\) describes variation not represented by the
  fitted model.

Every full and reduced model uses the same observations, outcome distribution,
link function, and participant structure. Site and day length share
information, so their part \(R^2\) values describe unique contributions and
are reported separately rather than added. The calculations are made for
every declared full model, regardless of whether its adjusted \(p\)-value is
below 0.05; the submitted significance-dependent switching is removed.

All effect estimates, model-based averages, marginal and conditional \(R^2\),
participant variance, and part \(R^2\) values receive 95% confidence
intervals. The intervals will be obtained from at least 1,000 successful
parametric-bootstrap refits per metric, with the random seed and failed refits
recorded. Full and reduced models are refitted within the same bootstrap
replicate so uncertainty in an \(R^2\) difference is calculated directly.
The Tweedie-model \(R^2\) values are summaries on the model's log-link scale;
the primary calculation uses the lognormal residual-variance approximation,
with the delta approximation as a named sensitivity.

## Direct result comparison

During implementation, every metric will be compared through four explicit
stages:

1. the saved or reported manuscript result, for audit discussion;
2. the main H01 implementation using the newly prepared data;
3. the same H01 implementation using the manuscript-prepared dataset, with
   only objective data errors corrected; and
4. paired/common-sample near-eye and complementary chest results.

Each participant-day comparison row will include the exact participants,
participant-days (model rows), and sites used by the model, overall and by
site. Each participant-level IS or IV row will include the participants (model
rows), contributing participant-days, and sites, overall and by site. The main
analysis also reports the valid measurement hours contributing to each metric.
Those exact hours were not retained with the manuscript-prepared metric
artifacts and are therefore labelled as unavailable in that sensitivity,
never as zero. Measurement hours are derivation support, not additional model
rows. The table will also include the estimate, standard error, 95% confidence interval,
interval method, raw \(p\)-value, submitted adjusted \(p\)-value where
recoverable, main and manuscript-prepared-data adjusted \(p\)-values, the
17-test family and its size, the result's position after sorting its
\(p\)-values, \(R^2\), whether the model fitted stably, diagnostic status,
direction, practical magnitude, change in statistical significance or
conclusion, and manuscript-claim change. The main-versus-sensitivity comparison
will also report the exact shared participants and participant-days.

No main or manuscript-prepared-data H01 value is available yet. Result and
claim differences therefore remain `pending`, not `unchanged`.

## Why the method changes

The review of predictor structure, conducted without examining rebuilt H01
outcome results, established that:

- site and day length can be estimated together;
- separate site, latitude, and day-length effects cannot all be estimated
  together because latitude is constant within each site;
- a latitude coefficient cannot be interpreted after including a separate
  term for every site; and
- the site-adjusted day-length coefficient is estimated mainly from uneven
  within-site collection periods, with very little variation at some sites.

Accordingly, the main-analysis claim would be framed as:

> Site differences were not fully summarized by latitude and observed
> photoperiod.

It would not say that a site effect persisted after adjustment for latitude.

## Diagnostics and sensitivities

Mandatory checks include use of the same observations in each model
comparison; metric-specific sample flow; data coverage and transformation;
stable model fitting, including whether random effects can be estimated;
whether the selected probability distribution adequately describes the
residuals, which are the differences between observed and fitted values;
participant and site influence; leave-one-site-out latitude estimates,
obtained by omitting each site in turn; within-site day-length variation;
equal-site versus observed-sample averaging; and paired/common-sample placement
comparisons.

The all-outcome photoperiod adjustment is approved as the primary analysis
because it preserves the manuscript-generating method. The narrower literal
preregistration scope will be a named sensitivity. Material disagreement
requires the H01 decision to be reviewed again.

## Relation to the preregistration

The signed H01 stated that site differences would be assessed after
considering latitude and that photoperiod would be included for metrics with a
day/night-duration component. The manuscript-generating method applied
photoperiod to all seventeen outcomes and did not fit site and latitude
jointly.

The main method retains the manuscript-generating all-outcome photoperiod
analysis as primary, records it as a preregistration adaptation, and runs the narrower
registered scope as a sensitivity. The site-versus-latitude comparison is
clarified as a comparison of two models fitted to the same observations---one
using site and one using latitude---rather than a model containing both site
and latitude.

## Checks completed and approved decisions

The review of predictor structure used only site, participant, placement, date,
latitude, and day length. It verified 811 near-eye participant-days from 141
participants at nine sites and 897 chest participant-days from 154
participants at eight sites, with every row matched once to site and solar
context.

The author approved the following package before H01 fitting:

1. fixed site plus centered photoperiod as the primary model;
2. participant-mean photoperiod for participant-level IS and IV;
3. a latitude model using the same participant-days and participant random
   structure as the site model, with no random site intercept;
4. a separate descriptive random-site model rather than using random site in
   the latitude comparison;
5. all-outcome photoperiod adjustment as primary and the narrower registered
   scope as sensitivity;
6. four separate 17-value Benjamini--Hochberg families, each containing one
   preselected model-level test per metric, for site, photoperiod, latitude,
   and the formal same-frame site-versus-latitude adequacy comparison;
7. the hierarchical `emmeans` follow-up described above, with nine
   equally weighted from-mean site contrasts adjusted together within each
   metric and 95% confidence intervals for all estimates;
8. the marginal, conditional, participant, and part-\(R^2\) approach described
   above, with joint 95% bootstrap confidence intervals and a delta-method
   sensitivity for Tweedie-model \(R^2\); and
9. exact fitted-model sample sizes and supporting measurement hours overall
   and by site, using the units described above; and
10. the complete 17-metric response-family package described above; and
11. wording about whether latitude summarizes the site pattern only after the
   formal fourth family and its diagnostics have been evaluated.
